content: In cystic fibrosis (CF), airway obstruction and recurrent respiratory infections lead to chronic inflammation, progressive lung damage, respiratory failure, and ultimately death. Anti-inflammatory treatments, such as oral corticosteroids, are used because inflammation begins early in the disease process. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of long-term oral corticosteroid use (over 30 days) in managing respiratory complications in CF, with a focus on lung function and adverse effects. The review included randomized trials comparing oral corticosteroids administered for more than 30 days with either placebo or no additional therapy in individuals with CF. A total of eleven studies were identified, but only three studies, involving 354 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two of these studies had a four-year follow-up period, while one had a 12-week follow-up period. Due to differences in how outcomes were measured and reported, meta-analyses could not be performed. One study demonstrated that oral corticosteroids, at a prednisolone-equivalent dose of 1 mg/kg administered on alternate days, slowed the progression of lung disease. At two and four years, the percentage of predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) showed significantly greater improvement in the 1 mg/kg group compared to the placebo group (P < 0.02). However, during the first two years, the 2 mg/kg group did not show a significant difference compared to the placebo group. Adverse effects were notable. Linear growth retardation was observed as early as six months in the 2 mg/kg alternate-day prednisolone group and at 24 months in the 1 mg/kg alternate-day group. One four-year study was terminated early due to adverse events. A follow-up at year 10 revealed that catch-up growth began approximately two years after treatment cessation. However, alternate-day corticosteroid treatment appeared to impair growth in boys until adulthood. The authors concluded that oral corticosteroids at prednisolone-equivalent doses of 1 to 2 mg/kg administered on alternate days may slow the progression of lung disease in CF. However, this potential benefit must be carefully weighed against the risk of adverse effects, particularly growth impairment. A thorough risk-benefit analysis is essential when considering low-dose alternate-day corticosteroid therapy. No further trials of this intervention are anticipated, and the review will no longer be regularly updated. However, any newly published data will be incorporated if available.
